newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil not about to arrest train-robber Biggs.
newsitem.headline: Brazil not about to arrest train-robber Biggs.

text.p: Ronnie Biggs, Britain's most famous fugitive, is not about to be arrested by Brazilian police despite the ratification of an extradition treaty between the two countries on Wednesday.

"He won't be arrested immediately even if Britain issues an extradition request on Wednesday," a Brazilian Foreign Ministry said spokeswoman on Monday. "First we would have to analyse the case before issuing an order for his arrest."
Biggs, who fled to the safe refuge of Rio de Janeiro 27 years ago to escape a long jail term for his part in the legendary "Great Train Robbery", has hired lawyers to fight any extradition attempt.

The ageing thief, who turned 68 on Aug. 8, the 34th anniversary of the "Great Train Robbery", fears that when Brazil ratifies the 1995 extradition treaty on Wednesday he will be forced to return to Britain to serve out his 30-year prison sentence.
But any extradition promises to be a drawn-out affair.

The Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said Brazilian authorities would first have to investigate whether the case might constitute an act of political persecution or violation of human rights, and whether there were valid grounds on which to arrest Biggs.
Finally, the president of Brazil's highest court, the Supreme Federal Tribunal, would have to decide whether or not to issue an order for his arrest, she said.
Biggs was a member of a gang that in 1963 stole 2.6 million pounds -- the equivalent of about 30 million pounds ($48 million) at today's values -- from a Royal Mail train.
The gang, whose heist was made into a movie, was captured but Biggs scaled the walls of a London jail and escaped in 1965 after serving only 15 months of his jail term.
After plastic surgery to change his appearance and hiding out in Australia, Biggs settled in Brazil, a popular haven for international fugitives because of its lack of extradition laws.

His safety was further guaranteed when his son Michael was born, because under Brazilian law Biggs could not be touched as long as he had a dependent. His son, who will turn 23 next month, is now legally independent.
Biggs, who has led a crime-free life since arriving in Brazil, has hired Brazilian and British lawyers to fight for his freedom in the courts, and believes luck is on his side.

"I have infinite faith that I won't go to jail," Biggs told Reuters during a recent interview at his home overlooking Rio. "I have been lucky until today and I hope I will continue to be lucky. In Brazil, everything is forgiven and forgotten after 20 years."

He has infuriated the authorities over the years by flaunting his freedom, appearing on television to promote his autobiography and living in an apartment with a giant British flag signed by his many visitors.
